issues.legal_issue: A development plan is not unconstitutional merely because a landowner is not given a separate opportunity to respond to modifications made after objections or suggestions from others.
material_facts: The landowners challenged changes made to a development plan after its initial publication, including the designation of land for public purposes.
The plan covered a very large urban area and a large population, and its preparation required extensive surveys and planning.

The authorities publicized the planning process, considered objections and suggestions at different stages, used advisory and expert committees, and had objections scrutinized before the plan was sanctioned.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a separate hearing for every affected owner on modifications made after considering other persons’ suggestions did not make the challenged provisions invalid under Articles 14 or 19.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 9 and 10 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 permitted the local authority to consider public suggestions and modify the plan before submission, and the State Government to sanction it with modifications. The Court held that the planning task and its public purpose did not require separate hearings for every person affected by each suggestion or modification, where the process involved public participation and careful consideration. It relied on the approach to legislative guidance and restrictions in Jyoti Pershad v. Administration for the Union Territory of Delhi, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 125, and on the treatment of publicity and objections in Manecklal Chhotalal v. M. G. Makwana, [1967] 3 S.C.R. 65.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_development_: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law governing preparation and approval of a development plan.
predicates.development_plan_may_be_modified_after_p: The planning process allows authorities to revise a plan after receiving suggestions or objections from members of the public.
predicates.large_scale_planning_task: The plan concerns a large area or population and requires extensive planning work.
predicates.objections_considered_through_public_pro: Authorities publicize the planning process and consider objections or suggestions, with assistance from committees or experts where appropriate.
predicates.affected_owner_not_separately_heard_on_e: An owner affected by a change is not separately heard on each modification prompted by another person’s suggestion or objection.

issues.definition: When a public process considers objections and suggestions as part of a large-scale planning task, the lack of a separate hearing for each affected owner on each modification does not by itself invalidate the plan.

issues.legal_issue: The power to grant or refuse permission for development is not arbitrary merely because the law provides no appeal, where the statutory planning framework and required inquiry guide the decision.
material_facts: The landowners sought permission to develop land after the planning process had begun, and their applications for commencement certificates were refused.
Tentative plans and, later, a final development plan provided material relevant to the proposed development.
The governing law required an inquiry before a commencement certificate was granted or refused, and the decisions were made by senior officers closely connected with preparation of the plan.
The law did not provide an appeal or revision from the decision on a commencement certificate.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge to the relevant powers under sections 12 and 13, holding that they were not uncanalised or arbitrary and that the absence of an appeal did not make them invalid under Articles 14 or 19.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 13 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 required an application for a commencement certificate and an inquiry before it was granted or refused. The Court held that the Act’s planning purpose, the tentative and final plans, and the requirement to consider available material supplied adequate guidance. It considered the decision-maker’s senior position and connection with preparation of the plan relevant to the objection that no appeal or revision was provided. The Court applied the guidance principles discussed in Jyoti Pershad v. Administration for the Union Territory of Delhi, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 125, and relied on Manecklal Chhotalal v. M. G. Makwana, [1967] 3 S.C.R. 65, in considering the Act’s planning framework.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_development_: A person challenges the constitutionality of a legal power to grant or refuse permission for development.
predicates.development_permission_application_after: A person applies to develop land after the authority has announced its intention to prepare a development plan.
predicates.inquiry_required_before_decision: The governing process requires the authority to inquire before deciding whether to grant development permission.
predicates.planning_material_guides_decision: Tentative or final planning materials relevant to the proposed development are available to guide the decision.
predicates.decision_made_by_senior_planning_authori: A senior local-authority officer connected with the planning process makes the decision.
predicates.no_appeal_provided: The governing process does not provide an appeal or revision from the decision.

issues.definition: Where a guided planning process requires an inquiry and a senior planning authority decides the application, the absence of an appeal does not by itself make the development-permission power invalid as arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: The period allowed for acquiring land designated for a public purpose is not an unreasonable restriction on property rights when the scale and financing demands of the planning task make that period reasonable.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the time allowed for acquiring land designated for public purposes, arguing that the combined planning and acquisition process could delay acquisition for many years and potentially longer if the plan were revised.
The development plan concerned an area of about 169 square miles, and the local authority faced substantial practical and financial demands in acquiring land for public purposes.
The statutory scheme included a time limit for acquisition and a mechanism by which the designation could lapse if acquisition steps were not taken after the prescribed process.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the acquisition period was not too long in the circumstances and did not constitute an unreasonable restriction on the right to hold property; it did not decide the validity of the provision concerning revision of development plans.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the combined operation of sections 4, 10(3), and 11(3) of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, including the time allowed for acquisition and the mechanism for lapse of a designation. It held that the time was reasonable in light of the large planning area, the need to prepare and implement a development plan, and the local authority’s limited resources. It relied on the reasoning in Jyoti Pershad v. Administration for the Union Territory of Delhi, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 125, concerning restrictions assessed in light of practical circumstances and statutory purpose. The Court expressly left the validity of section 17 undecided.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_res: A person challenges a restriction on property rights arising from a town-planning scheme.
predicates.land_designated_for_public_purpose: The planning authority designates privately held land for a public purpose.
predicates.large_scale_planning_and_acquisition_tas: The authority must plan and acquire land across a large area or for extensive public needs.
predicates.acquisition_requires_substantial_public_: Acquisition depends on public funds that the authority cannot deploy all at once.
predicates.scheme_provides_time_limit_and_lapse_saf: The scheme allows a period for acquisition and provides a process by which the designation may lapse if acquisition steps are not taken.

issues.definition: Where public-purpose acquisition forms part of a large, resource-intensive planning task and the scheme includes a time limit and lapse safeguard, the acquisition period is not an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
